Actually, this is a marketing ploy!

In 1938, DeBeers was seeing slumping sales of diamonds and they wanted to increase the market. They began an ad campaign educating the public about the various metrics for the quality of diamonds, and positioned the engagement ring as a form of dowry, suggesting that you should (and must) prove your dedication to providing for your wife by buying her the nicest ring you could manage. It's explained more thoroughly in the wikipedia page.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagement_ring#20th_century

It is NOT bad if you choose wisely and go for simple and affordable. As a matter of fact I think more of people that go that route.

The actual purpose of engagement and wedding rings being gold-and-diamond is pretty straightforward: 1) the man can afford to buy the ring, so he can support his wife and eventual family; the more expensive the ring, the bigger a catch he is and the more incentive the woman has to accept his offer of marriage; 2) if the man dies and the woman falls on hard times, she can sell the ring; if she is unfaithful or some such, he can take back and sell the ring. Gold and diamonds have both been consistently valuable over time, so it's always been considered a good investment.

These are just straightforward observations/pragmatism. In MY opinion, the ring thing has outlived its usefulness and appeal. Other than its ability to be recognized as a sign that someone is 'taken', I don't really appreciate the ring itself. There are many ways to create and wear lasting symbols of a union, and they are not all so expensive or able to be stolen. Buying a ring, to buy a ring, isn't necessarily embracing the meaning and essence of a relationship.

I like tattoos for this purpose! They're not really a symbol of marriage, but they're permanently on your body, can be customized, can't easily (or reasonably) be stolen, and just like a divorce, you can seek removal but it's going to be painful and leave scars. I think that's beautiful.

Edit: BTW, I'm not saying the reasons I listed above are logical-- I'm saying that's the premise/thought process of what it's ostensibly supposed to be. Goodness knows I've known my share of dudes who saved up to buy rings they couldn't afford. I think they could've taken a nice vacation for the same price and gotten way more out of it together, but that's just me.

Does doing a secondary end up with less yeast during bottling?

Yes and no?

Yes in that if you're not careful when racking into the bottling bucket from the primary, you can add unwanted yeast. This is easy to mitigate though, just don't move the primary for a day before moving the beer and don't try for every last scrap of liquid. I like to swirl the primary Several days ahead and tilt it so the yeast falls mostly to one side, then change the tilt to the other side for moving the beer.

No in that there's always yeast in suspension and through the process needed to carbonate in the bottle (adding sugar to the wort/beer in the bottling bucket), you make the yeast active again where they eat and reproduce. That means you will always have yeast in the bottle if you carbonate in the bottle. The only way around it is to force carbonate (keg) and then fill the bottles (beer gun), ideally after running the beer through a particulate filter (before kegging).

There's really no reason for a homebrewer to do a secondary. Commercial breweries do it because in HUGE batches, the weight of the liquid can/does kill yeast cells when in a conical fermenter which then imparts off-flavors. That's not a condition that exists with 5gallon batches, or buckets/carboys.
The reason I want to do it is because my gut feels tender the day after drinking a homebrew.

The 2 things you can do then:

First, if you bottle, make sure the bottles sit for a couple months first so the yeast precipitates, then make sure not to shake them and pour off into a glass, leaving several ounces in the bottom.

Second, start kegging. With 2 kegs you can filter out ALL of the yeast. Even if you don't filter (I don't), if the keg sits for several weeks, only the first couple of pours will have anything in them (clearing the pick-up) and then you can enjoy the remaining ~40 pours (the last one will have some in it as well).

The more you rack beer, the more you open yourself up for oxidization (skunking).
